sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E1687. Attribution follows conversational continuity and the supplied anchors, not ideological content. The transcript contains substantial recognition errors, no explicit speaker labels, and several events crossing speaker changes; these are marked U where inseparable. Quotations preserve the supplied text. No identifiable edited replay was found: the opening presentation continues into the debate rather than repeating later speech.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: secular humanist pick one pick one
candidates.explanation: The catchphrase presents secular humanism as incoherent. Its immediate genealogical reason (E161–165) does not establish that secular justification is impossible. However, B supplies additional grounding arguments about incarnation and humanity (E190–228), making substitution uncertain rather than confirmed. No objection is expressly disqualified; B later invites possible non-theistic examples (E740–742).

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: God can ground goodness but I would argue he can only ground goodness in the same way
contrasts.explanation: A develops the comparison through two alternatives: grounding God's goodness in another property or treating goodness as basic. He expressly denies that this defeats religious morality or makes it unsophisticated (E570–585). The conclusion summarizes reasons and qualifications.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: Jesus himself told us to read the Bible in a certain way
contrasts.explanation: B answers the Old Testament objection with a specific interpretive argument from Matthew 19, acknowledging nonideal laws and conduct (E1488–1514). This offers an assessable reason for developmental interpretation; it does not explicitly make every possible moral objection irrelevant.
